standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: Keeping the partnership and intimacy alive with kids in the picture; co-parenting connection and communication under load (UNESCO 1.2, 5.3, 7.1). New v2 build, opening Chapter 8 (Parenthood) with the relationship parenting strains most: the couple's own, and the self within it. A baby changes everything, including you two. Six modes: the big shift (a baby reshapes the couple and each self, normalised, around two in three couples feel the dip and it isn't a verdict; the thrivers use learnable skills, not luck), talk through the tired (communication and repair under exhaustion, name the tiredness not each other, appreciation, assume good intent; bust 'the romance is just over'), share don't resent (fair division as the strongest relationship protector, a partner's involvement is practical and symbolic 'this is ours, not yours'; engage fathers directly, co-parenting is not a mothers-only topic, a father isn't 'babysitting' his own child; links Equal Parents g62), reconnecting (rebuilding emotional and physical intimacy at the pace of both partners' readiness, no deadline and no obligation, frank but respectful, recovery is individual; postpartum discomfort routes to a clinician), you still matter (protecting each partner's identity and wellbeing, you're still a whole person not only a parent, the 'I used to be someone else' shift is common, ask how the parent is not just the baby; persistent low mood routes to Looking After You g63), tools and help (a daily check-in and reconnect toolkit, protected couple time even in a joint family, and routes). Even-handed and warm: engages fathers as equal parents, offers partnership not pity, applies no pressure on intimacy timing, and is frank but respectful; not medical advice. Builds on Choosing & Building (g53) and Real Relationships (g46); links Equal Parents (g62), Looking After You (g63), The Family Map (g57) and Respect at Home (g56). India: a new baby often arrives within a joint family, bringing help but also pressure and less couple privacy, and postpartum women face a dual burden, role conflict and guilt; relationship strain that turns to control or abuse routes to Respect at Home (g56) and help.

evidenceBase: The transition to parenthood strains the couple, and that strain is common rather than a verdict: longitudinal research (Gottman and others) finds around two-thirds of couples report a dip in relationship satisfaction after a first child, steepest in the first year, while the roughly one-third who maintain or improve do so through specific learnable skills and intentional choices, not luck, personality or an easier baby. Parenthood also shifts each partner's identity, and feeling 'I used to be someone else' is a common, normal part of the change, so the node normalises the upheaval and frames it as workable as a team (Gottman transition-to-parenthood research; postpartum identity studies)

Communication and a fairly shared load are the strongest protectors of the post-baby couple: exhaustion, not the partner, is the enemy, so naming tiredness, pausing hard talks for calmer moments, repairing quickly and expressing appreciation (even small and imperfect) keep the bond alive, while a partner's genuine involvement in the household and childcare is one of the strongest predictors of relationship satisfaction, both practically and symbolically, signalling 'this is ours, not yours'. The framing engages fathers directly, treats co-parenting as a both-parents topic rather than a mothers-only one, rejects the idea that a father caring for his own child is 'babysitting', and offers partnership rather than pity (Gottman protective factors; division-of-labour and mental-load research)

Intimacy and each partner's wellbeing rebuild best with patience and no pressure: physical recovery after childbirth is individual and intimacy returns at the pace of both partners' physical and emotional readiness rather than on a schedule or by obligation, with emotional reconnection usually leading and postpartum discomfort being common and treatable by a clinician. Each parent also remains a whole person who is steadier for keeping some of their own self, new parents (especially the one recovering) often feel unseen so asking 'how are you?' matters, and persistent low mood after birth is real and routes to postpartum wellbeing support (Looking After You g63), while strain that turns to control or abuse routes to Respect at Home (g56); the content is frank but respectful and is not medical advice (postpartum recovery and perinatal mental-health guidance; UNESCO relationships)

scenarios.hook: "If our relationship struggles after the baby, it means we're failing."
scenarios.relearn: Most couples feel the strain after a baby; it's common and normal, not a sign you're failing.

myth.un: If our relationship struggles after the baby, it means we're failing.
myth.re: Around two in three couples find their satisfaction dips after a first child; the strain is common, not a verdict on your love.
myth.why: Knowing it's normal takes the panic out of it.

scenarios.hook: "The couples who stay happy after kids just got lucky with an easy baby."
scenarios.relearn: Couples who thrive after kids use learnable skills, not luck or an easier baby.

myth.un: The couples who stay happy after kids just got lucky with an easy baby.
myth.re: The couples who thrive aren't luckier; they use specific skills, sharing the load, communicating and appreciating each other.
myth.why: It's skills you can learn, not luck.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a normal part of the new-baby shift, or a sign something's truly wrong?
scenarios.relearn: Tiredness and more friction are normal adjustment; control, threats and constant put-downs are not, and need help.

items.text: Feeling tired and short on couple time
Being controlled or frightened by your partner
More friction while you adjust
Threats or being put down constantly

scenarios.hook: Since the baby, you and your partner feel more like exhausted teammates than lovers, and it scares you.
scenarios.relearn: Name the post-baby shift as a normal phase to work on together, not a crisis to withdraw from.

options.text: Name it together as a normal phase you'll actively work through
options.consequence: You face the shift as a team, not a crisis.

options.text: Assume the relationship is over and withdraw
options.consequence: Naming it as a normal, workable phase faces it together; assuming it's over and withdrawing makes the distance real.

scenarios.debrief: Treat the post-baby dip as a normal phase to work through together, not proof the relationship is over.

scenarios.hook: Match each part of the big shift to the reassuring truth.
scenarios.relearn: The dip in time, the sense of change and the extra friction are all normal parts of becoming parents.

pairs.left: Less time and energy for each other
pairs.right: Common, and it eases as you adapt
New parents do change; that's normal
Friction while adjusting isn't the end

scenarios.hook: "Becoming a parent shouldn't change who I am at all."
scenarios.relearn: Parenthood shifts your identity; feeling changed is normal, and you can hold both who you were and who you're becoming.

myth.un: Becoming a parent shouldn't change who I am at all.
myth.re: Parenthood does shift your identity, and feeling 'I used to be someone else' is common; you can hold both selves.
myth.why: Acknowledging the change helps you adapt.

scenarios.hook: Sam: a baby reshapes you two and each of you; knowing that's normal is the first relief. Land okay?
scenarios.relearn: The post-baby reshaping of you two, and of each of you, is normal; knowing that is the first relief.
scenarios.affirm: Knowing the post-baby reshaping of the couple and the self is normal removes a lot of needless fear.

scenarios.hook: Spot the healthy way to meet the big shift.
scenarios.relearn: Meet the big shift with patience and teamwork, not by reading every hard day as doom.

scene.text: Expecting an adjustment and teaming up
Reading every hard day as doom
Being patient with each other and yourselves

scenarios.why: Expecting adjustment, teaming up and patience are healthy; reading every hard day as doom isn't.

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself comparing your tired, messy reality to glossy 'perfect new parents' online.
scenarios.relearn: Ignore the 'perfect parents' highlight reel; your real, messy progress is the only fair measure.

options.text: Tune out the highlight reel and judge by your own real progress
options.consequence: You drop a needless extra weight.

options.text: Feel you're failing for not matching the feed
options.consequence: Tuning out the highlight reel lifts a false standard; comparing to curated perfection only adds shame to exhaustion.

scenarios.debrief: Don't measure your real new-parent life against curated online perfection; judge by your own progress.

scenarios.hook: Sam: you're not a worse couple now, you're a couple under new load. Big difference. Feel it?
scenarios.relearn: You're not a worse couple now, just one under new load, and that's something you can work with.
scenarios.affirm: You're not a worse couple after a baby; you're a couple carrying new load, which is workable.

scenarios.hook: "Once you have kids, the romance and real talking are just over."
scenarios.relearn: Romance and real talking aren't over after kids; small, intentional connection keeps the bond alive.

myth.un: Once you have kids, the romance and real talking are just over.
myth.re: Connection changes shape but isn't over; small, intentional communication and appreciation keep the bond alive.
myth.why: The bond is maintained, not finished.

scenarios.hook: "When we're both exhausted, snapping at each other is just unavoidable."
scenarios.relearn: Snapping isn't unavoidable; name the exhaustion, not each other, and hold hard talks for calmer moments.

myth.un: When we're both exhausted, snapping at each other is just unavoidable.
myth.re: Exhaustion is the enemy, not your partner; naming the tiredness and pausing hard talks for calmer moments protects you both.
myth.why: Aim the frustration at the problem, not the person.

scenarios.hook: A small thing flares into a fight, but really you're both just running on no sleep.
scenarios.relearn: Pause depleted fights and revisit rested; don't try to win an argument that's really just tiredness.

options.text: Pause and say 'we're both exhausted, let's revisit this rested'
options.consequence: You stop the spiral before it wounds.

options.text: Push the argument to 'win' it while depleted
options.consequence: Pausing till you're rested stops the spiral; pushing to win while depleted says things you'll both regret.

scenarios.debrief: When a fight is really exhaustion talking, pause and revisit it rested rather than pushing to win.

scenarios.hook: Match each communication habit to what it protects after a baby.
scenarios.relearn: Naming tiredness, repairing fast and appreciating each other are the habits that protect a couple under load.

scenarios.hook: "Saying thank you for ordinary parenting stuff is unnecessary."
scenarios.relearn: Appreciation, even for ordinary parenting work, is one of the strongest ways couples stay close after kids.

myth.un: Saying thank you for ordinary parenting stuff is unnecessary.
myth.re: Expressing appreciation, even small and imperfect, is one of the strongest things that keeps couples close through this phase.

scenarios.hook: Your partner has been quietly carrying a lot. You want to make them feel seen.
scenarios.relearn: Naming what they do and that you're in it together makes a depleted partner feel seen and held.

yourLine.text: "I see how much you're doing, and I'm grateful, we're in this together."
"This is just what parents do, no need to make a thing of it."

scenarios.hook: Spot the move that helps a hard conversation under exhaustion.
scenarios.relearn: Help hard talks land by choosing a calmer moment and a soft start, not a depleted 3am ambush.

scene.text: Picking a calmer moment to talk
Launching a serious talk at 3am, depleted
Leading with 'I' and a soft start

scenarios.why: A calmer moment and a soft start help; launching a serious talk depleted at 3am rarely goes well.

scenarios.hook: You're hurt by something your partner said while frazzled, and resentment is building.
scenarios.relearn: Raise hurts calmly, assuming good intent; storing them as a case against your partner corrodes the team.

options.text: Raise it gently once you're both calmer, assuming good intent
options.consequence: You clear the air without a blow-up.

options.text: Store it up as evidence against them
options.consequence: Raising it calmly with good intent clears the air; storing it as evidence builds a case that poisons the team.

scenarios.debrief: Raise hurts gently when calm and assume good intent; don't store them up as evidence.

scenarios.hook: Sam: under sleep deprivation, assume your partner is tired, not against you. Worth holding onto?
scenarios.relearn: Under exhaustion, assume your partner is tired, not against you; it defuses most conflicts.
scenarios.affirm: Assuming good intent, that your partner is tired rather than against you, prevents most exhausted conflicts.

scenarios.hook: Match a frazzled moment to a kinder response.
scenarios.relearn: Each frazzled moment has a kinder response that protects the couple instead of escalating.

pairs.left: A serious issue keeps colliding with chaos
pairs.right: "Let's set ten calm minutes for this."

scenarios.hook: "The mother is the natural default parent; the father just helps out."
scenarios.relearn: Both are real parents; fairly sharing the load, not 'helping out', strongly protects the relationship.

myth.un: The mother is the natural default parent; the father just helps out.
myth.re: Both parents are real parents; sharing the load fairly, not 'helping', is one of the strongest protectors of the relationship.
myth.why: Co-parenting is shared ownership, not assistance.

scenarios.hook: "A father looking after his own child is 'babysitting'."
scenarios.relearn: A father caring for his child is parenting, not babysitting; it's his own job, not a favour.

myth.un: A father looking after his own child is 'babysitting'.
myth.re: It's just parenting; a father caring for his child is doing his own job, not doing anyone a favour.
myth.why: You don't babysit your own kid.

scenarios.hook: Sort: shared parenting that protects the couple, or a lopsided load that breeds resentment?
scenarios.relearn: Both tracking and doing, and fair splits, protect the couple; one carrying it all or only 'helping when asked' breeds resentment.

One parent silently carrying it all
Splitting nights and tasks fairly

scenarios.hook: You realise one of you is carrying almost all the baby load and quietly resenting it.
scenarios.relearn: Make the load visible and share it fairly; silent resentment is what eventually explodes.

options.text: Let it build silently until it explodes
options.consequence: Making the load visible and renegotiating fixes the real problem; silent resentment grows until it bursts.

scenarios.debrief: Surface the full baby load and renegotiate a fair split before resentment builds and bursts.

scenarios.hook: Match each kind of post-baby work to the fair approach.
scenarios.relearn: Night wake-ups, the mental load and the chores are all fairer when owned together, not dumped on one parent.

pairs.right: Shared or alternated, not one person's

pairs.left: The mental load of tracking needs
pairs.right: Both notice and plan, not one manager
Owned in fair shares, not 'helped' with

scenarios.hook: "Co-parenting and load-sharing are really mothers' topics."
scenarios.relearn: Co-parenting isn't a mothers-only topic; a father's real involvement strongly predicts a happy couple.

myth.un: Co-parenting and load-sharing are really mothers' topics.
myth.re: Co-parenting is for both parents directly; a father's involvement in the load is a top predictor of a happy couple.

scenarios.hook: Sam: sharing the load isn't just practical, it says 'this is ours, not yours'. Feel the difference?
scenarios.relearn: Sharing the load says 'this is ours, not yours', which protects the couple as much as the practical help does.
scenarios.affirm: Sharing the load is practical and symbolic: it tells your partner the children are 'ours', not their sole burden.

scenarios.hook: Spot what genuinely shares the parenting load.
scenarios.relearn: Truly sharing the load means owning tasks unprompted and holding the mental load, not waiting to be told.

scene.text: Owning whole tasks without being asked
Waiting to be told each step

scenarios.why: Owning whole tasks unprompted and sharing the mental load genuinely share the work; waiting to be told doesn't.

scenarios.hook: Relatives praise your partner lavishly for doing the basic parenting you do daily unremarked.
scenarios.relearn: Reset the gendered double standard kindly; the same ordinary parenting deserves the same recognition.

options.text: Gently reset the frame: this is shared, ordinary parenting for you both
options.consequence: You keep the standard equal for both parents.

options.text: Let the gendered double standard stand
options.consequence: Resetting the frame keeps the standard equal; letting the double standard stand quietly devalues the default parent.

scenarios.debrief: Push back kindly on the double standard that praises a father for the parenting a mother does unremarked.

scenarios.hook: Sam: the fairer the load, the warmer the couple; this is the strongest protector there is. Worth prioritising?
scenarios.relearn: The fairer the load, the warmer the couple; sharing it is the strongest protector there is.
scenarios.affirm: A fairly shared load is one of the strongest protectors of post-baby relationship satisfaction.

scenarios.hook: "After a baby, you owe each other sex again by a set date."
scenarios.relearn: Intimacy after a baby has no deadline; it returns at both partners' physical and emotional readiness, never by obligation.

myth.un: After a baby, you owe each other sex again by a set date.
myth.re: There's no deadline; intimacy returns at the pace of both partners' physical and emotional readiness, never on a schedule or by obligation.

scenarios.hook: "Wanting to wait for intimacy after birth means something is wrong with you."
scenarios.relearn: Needing time for intimacy after birth is normal and healthy; recovery is individual, not a problem with you.

myth.un: Wanting to wait for intimacy after birth means something is wrong with you.
myth.re: Recovery is individual and bodies and feelings differ; needing time, often weeks or more, is normal and healthy, not a problem.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy way to rebuild closeness after kids, or pressure to avoid?
scenarios.relearn: A shared pace and emotional reconnection first are healthy; pressuring an unready partner or treating intimacy as owed are not.

items.text: Going at a pace you both choose
Pressuring a partner who isn't ready
Reconnecting emotionally first
Treating intimacy as an obligation owed

scenarios.hook: You miss physical closeness, but your partner isn't ready yet after the birth.
scenarios.relearn: Reconnect gently and patiently; pushing an unready partner harms the very closeness you want.

options.text: Reconnect in small non-sexual ways and let intimacy return without pressure
options.consequence: Closeness rebuilds on a foundation of safety.

options.text: Push or guilt them into it before they're ready
options.consequence: Small non-sexual closeness rebuilds safely; pushing or guilting an unready partner damages trust and desire.

scenarios.debrief: Rebuild closeness without pressure, letting intimacy return when both are ready, not on demand.

scenarios.hook: Match each small reconnection to what it rebuilds.

pairs.left: A short walk or chat together

scenarios.hook: "Reconnecting means jumping straight back to how sex was before."

myth.un: Reconnecting means jumping straight back to how sex was before.
myth.re: Intimacy after kids often rebuilds gradually and may look different; communication and patience matter more than going 'back to before'.

scenarios.hook: You want to talk with your partner about reconnecting, without either of you feeling pressured.

scenarios.affirm: Closeness rebuilds best with emotional safety and no pressure; emotional reconnection tends to come first.

scenarios.hook: Intimacy after the birth is uncomfortable or painful and you're unsure if that's normal.

scenarios.hook: Sam: this is frank but yours to pace; nothing here is owed, and care is there if you need it. Feel respected?

scenarios.hook: "A good parent disappears completely into their children."

scenarios.hook: "Feeling like 'I used to be someone else' after a baby is shameful."

scenarios.relearn: Expecting less sleep and needing to adapt is fair; expecting nothing to change or instant perfection sets you up to hurt.

items.text: Less sleep and less couple time for a while
Everything staying exactly as before
Needing to adapt as a team
Feeling like perfect parents instantly

scenarios.hook: Sort: within the normal post-baby adjustment, or a reason to get support?
scenarios.relearn: Exhausted tears and more bickering are normal; weeks of numbness or frightening thoughts are reasons to get support.

items.text: Occasional tears from sheer exhaustion
Weeks of feeling numb or hopeless
Bickering more while sleep-starved
Frightening thoughts that worry you

scenarios.hook: Sam: the goal isn't to skip the hard part, it's to go through it as a team. Sit right?
scenarios.relearn: The goal isn't skipping the hard part, but going through it as a team.
scenarios.affirm: The aim isn't to avoid the hard transition but to move through it together, which keeps the couple whole.

scenarios.hook: You snapped at your partner over nothing while running on no sleep. You want to repair.
scenarios.relearn: A quick, honest repair, naming the exhaustion, mends a snap before it hardens into distance.

yourLine.text: "I'm sorry I snapped, that was the exhaustion talking, not how I feel about you."
"Well, you started it."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a soft start to a hard talk, or a harsh one that backfires?
scenarios.relearn: 'I'm struggling, can we find a calm minute' are soft starts; 'you never' and 'what is wrong with you' are harsh and backfire.

items.text: "I'm struggling and need your help with..."
"You never do anything around here."
"Can we find a calm minute to sort this?"
"What is wrong with you?"

scenarios.hook: Match each exhausted-couple trap to the skill that defuses it.
scenarios.relearn: Snapping, score-keeping and piling up hurts are each defused by naming tiredness, appreciating and repairing fast.

pairs.left: Keeping score of who did more

scenarios.hook: You and your partner keep having the same fight in circles, both too tired to resolve it.
scenarios.relearn: Park circular tired fights for a rested moment; midnight re-runs never resolve them.

options.text: Agree to park it and book ten calm minutes when you're both rested
options.consequence: You break the exhausted loop.

options.text: Keep re-running it at midnight
options.consequence: Parking it for a rested moment breaks the loop; re-running it depleted at midnight just deepens the rut.

scenarios.debrief: Break a circular tired fight by parking it for a calm, rested ten minutes, not re-running it depleted.

scenarios.hook: You want to step up as an equal parent, not a 'helper'. You tell your partner how you see it.
scenarios.relearn: Claiming the work as shared and owning it unasked turns a 'helper' into a true co-parent.

yourLine.text: "These aren't your jobs I help with, they're ours, I'll own my half without being asked."
"Just tell me what you want me to do."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a co-parenting move that shares the load, or one that quietly dumps it?
scenarios.relearn: Tracking needs yourself and taking whole nights share the load; waiting for a list and 'helping out' dump it on one parent.

items.text: Tracking the baby's needs yourself too
Waiting to be handed a task list
Taking whole nights in turn
Calling your own parenting 'helping out'

scenarios.hook: Your partner keeps managing everything and won't hand any of it over. You want to truly take a share.
scenarios.relearn: Offering to own a whole domain end-to-end lifts the mental load, not just the task, off your partner.

yourLine.text: "Let me fully own bath and bedtime, start to finish, so it's off your mind for good."
"Tell me if you need anything."

scenarios.hook: Match each parent's contribution to the respect it deserves.
scenarios.relearn: Night care, the mental load and daytime care are all real parenting work that deserves equal respect.

pairs.right: The mental load, shared not solo

pairs.left: Daytime care while the other works

scenarios.hook: You want your recovering partner to know there's zero pressure about intimacy. You reassure them.
scenarios.relearn: A clear 'no clock, your pace' reassurance removes pressure and makes safe closeness possible.

yourLine.text: "There's no clock here, we go at your pace, I just want to feel close in whatever way works."
"So when are things going back to normal?"

scenarios.hook: Sort: rebuilds closeness safely, or pressures a recovering partner?
scenarios.relearn: Letting readiness lead and agenda-free affection rebuild safely; hinting they're overdue or sulking is pressure.

items.text: Letting readiness lead, both ways
Hinting they're overdue
Cuddles and talk with no agenda
Sulking when they're not ready

scenarios.hook: Sam: feeling close again often starts with a laugh or a hug, long before anything else. Reassuring?
scenarios.relearn: Feeling close again often starts with a laugh or a hug, long before anything else.
scenarios.affirm: Reconnection usually starts with small emotional closeness, a laugh or a hug, well before physical intimacy.

scenarios.hook: Spot the pressure-free way to rebuild intimacy.
scenarios.relearn: Rebuild intimacy by following readiness and talking openly, never by setting a deadline.

scene.text: Setting a deadline to 'get back to normal'
Talking openly about what feels right

scenarios.why: Following readiness and talking openly are pressure-free; setting a 'back to normal' deadline isn't.

scenarios.hook: Your partner hasn't had a moment to themselves in weeks. You want to give them a real break.
scenarios.relearn: A real, no-strings break that says 'you matter too' refuels your partner and protects the person they are.

yourLine.text: "Go take two hours that are just yours, I've got the baby, you matter too."
"You can rest once everything's done."

scenarios.hook: A relative keeps asking only about the baby and never how the new mother is doing. You want to shift it.
scenarios.relearn: Redirecting attention to how the parent is counters the invisible-parent feeling that wears new parents down.

yourLine.text: "The baby's great, and how is Divya doing? She's been amazing and could use the asking."
"Yes, baby's fine, that's all that matters."

scenarios.hook: Sort: keeps a parent whole, or erases them into the role?
scenarios.relearn: A small personal thing and trading time off keep a parent whole; guilt over any need erases them into the role.

items.text: Holding onto one small personal thing
Guilt over any time for yourself
Partners trading time off
Believing needs make you a bad parent

scenarios.hook: Match each sign to what a depleted parent really needs.
scenarios.relearn: A depleted parent needs rest, to be seen, and space to keep some self, not more pressure.

pairs.left: Snappy and tearful from no rest

pairs.right: To be seen and asked about

pairs.left: Losing touch with who they are
pairs.right: Space to reclaim a little self

scenarios.hook: You feel guilty for wanting an hour to yourself away from the baby.
scenarios.relearn: Take the break without guilt; self-care refuels the parent, it doesn't betray the child.

options.text: Take the hour without guilt; a refuelled parent is a better parent
options.consequence: You return steadier and more present.

options.text: Deny yourself any break to prove devotion
options.consequence: Taking the hour refuels you to parent well; denying all rest to prove devotion just burns you out.

scenarios.debrief: Taking some time for yourself isn't a failure of devotion; a refuelled parent parents better.

scenarios.hook: You want to start a tiny nightly ritual to stay connected. You suggest it to your partner.
scenarios.relearn: A tiny, doable nightly ritual keeps the couple connected now, instead of waiting for a calm that never comes.

yourLine.text: "Each night, two minutes, one hard thing and one good thing each? Just to stay us."
"We'll talk properly when life calms down."

scenarios.hook: Your partner seems to be struggling more than 'just tired', and you want to gently open the door to help.
scenarios.relearn: A gentle, worried, 'shall we talk to someone together' opens the door to help without shame or dismissal.

yourLine.text: "I'm a bit worried about how heavy this feels for you, would it help to talk to someone together?"
"You'll be fine, everyone copes."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a green-flag couple habit after kids, or a pattern to change?
scenarios.relearn: Check-ins, appreciation and protected couple time are habits to keep; bottling up and a resentment ledger need changing.

items.text: Daily check-ins and appreciation
Bottling everything up
Protecting a little couple time
Keeping a silent resentment ledger

scenarios.hook: Sam: small habits, said out loud, beat grand gestures you never have energy for. Agree?
scenarios.relearn: Small habits done consistently beat grand gestures you never have the energy for.
scenarios.affirm: Small, consistent, spoken habits sustain a couple after kids better than grand gestures you can't sustain.
